title: Learner Autonomy in Practice

pts: Learner autonomy is the capacity to take charge of one's own learning — setting goals, choosing resources, evaluating progress.
It is not simply working unsupervised, which can happen with or without genuine autonomous capability.
This distinction matters for how autonomy is taught, not just permitted.
points.who: Henri Holec, "Autonomy and Foreign Language Learning"

v: A list of ten recent lessons or homework tasks

items: List ten recent tasks you set for one class.
For each, note who made five decisions: the goal, the content, the method, the pace, and how the work was evaluated.
Mark each decision T (teacher), L (learner) or S (shared).
Count the Ls and Ss.
Choose two decisions to share with learners next week.
Ask learners to fill in the same grid for a week of their own study and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A typical grid for a homework task (written for this book):

lines: Goal: T · Content: T · Method: T · Pace: L (they choose when to do it) · Evaluation: T

blocks.x: The learners work alone, but they make only one real decision. That is independence of place, not autonomy. A revised version:

lines: Goal: S (learners choose one of three aims) · Content: L (any short news text) · Method: T · Pace: L · Evaluation: S (self-check against a checklist, then teacher)

blocks.x: Holec’s (1981) definition makes the audit easy: count who takes charge.

body: Purpose: to separate working alone from taking charge. Content: two panels: a learner alone at a desk under a large pointing teacher’s hand; a learner in a group holding a plan she wrote herself. Style: clear contrast, captioned. Board version: two boxes labelled ‘Who decides?’.

items: Google Sheets (free) for the decision grid.

blocks.x: A five-column grid in the teaching journal.

pts: Unit 2 assessed autonomy readiness as part of the initial learner profile; this poster addresses actively building that capacity.
Autonomy develops incrementally through practice and reflection, not as a trait a learner either has or lacks permanently.
This reframes autonomy as a course outcome to teach toward, not just a precondition to plan around.

items: Draw a five-rung ladder: (1) follows instructions; (2) chooses between options the teacher gives; (3) adapts a task to suit themselves; (4) plans a short piece of learning with advice; (5) plans, carries out and evaluates independently.
Place each learner roughly on the ladder, using the Unit 2 readiness notes.
For each group of learners, plan one activity this month that invites them one rung higher.
Revisit the placements at the end of the term.
Share a simplified ladder with learners and ask them to place themselves.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Rung 1 → 2: Instead of one reading text, offer three at the same level and let learners choose.
Rung 2 → 3: Learners change one part of a task, such as the audience or the format.
Rung 3 → 4: Learners plan a week’s self-study with a short conference with the teacher.

blocks.x: The ladder reframes autonomy as a course outcome. A learner on rung 1 in June is at the start of a path, not outside it.

body: Purpose: to show autonomy as incremental. Content: a five-rung ladder with short labels; learners at different rungs, each reaching for the next, a teacher steadying the ladder. Style: encouraging. Board version: a ladder with five labelled rungs.

items: None needed; this is a planning task.

blocks.x: The ladder drawn in the teaching journal with learners’ initials.

pts: Explicitly teach how to set specific, achievable language-learning goals, connecting to Unit 47's micro-goal strategy.
Model the process of breaking a broad aim into concrete, trackable steps before expecting learners to do it independently.
Revisit and adjust goals periodically — autonomous goal-setting is an ongoing skill, not a one-time exercise.

items: Show a vague goal (‘I want better English’) and think aloud as you turn it into a specific goal.
Model the three questions: What exactly? By when? How will I know?
In pairs, learners turn two vague goals from a list into specific ones.
Each learner writes one four-week goal and three weekly steps.
After four weeks, learners review the goal; repeat monthly with less modelling each time.
Learners set goals in their home language first, then write the English version.
Support: a worksheet with the three questions and example answers.
Challenge: learners set a goal for their weakest skill.

lines: T: ‘I want better English.’ Better at what? Let’s say listening. Understanding the radio news. By when? In four weeks. How will I know? I’ll count how many stories I understand at the start and at the end.

blocks.x: A learner’s plan (written for this book):

lines: Four-week goal: Understand the main points of a five-minute English news bulletin.
Week 1: Listen to the slow news bulletin twice, with the transcript.
Weeks 2–4: Listen without the transcript and note three stories each time.

body: Purpose: to show goal-setting as a process. Content: a cloud labelled ‘I wish…’ turning into a target labelled with a specific goal, with three stepping stones leading to it. Style: bright, simple. Board version: cloud → target → three steps.

items: Google Keep (free) or a phone’s notes app for goal lists with checkboxes.

blocks.x: A goal page at the front of the notebook, reviewed monthly.

pts: Teach learners how to evaluate the quality and appropriateness of self-study resources, rather than assuming they already know how.
This connects to Unit 19's self-study strategy training, extended into a more deliberate evaluative skill.
A learner who can independently judge whether a resource suits their level and goal has a durable, transferable skill.

v: Four self-study resources (a graded reader, a news website, a video channel, a grammar app)

items: Show four resources learners might use at home.
Introduce four evaluation questions (see model language).
In groups, learners evaluate one resource each and report back.
Each learner chooses one resource for the coming month and writes a short reason.
Learners bring a resource they already use and evaluate it with the same questions.
Support: give a simple table with smiley faces for each question.
Challenge: learners write a 100-word review of a resource for younger learners.

blocks.x: Four evaluation questions (written for this book):

lines: Level: Do I understand about 90–95 per cent of it without a dictionary?
Purpose: Does it help with my goal?
Quality: Is the English accurate and natural? Who made it?
Habit: Can I use it regularly, with the time and devices I actually have?
A: The grammar app is fun, but it only has gap-fills.
B: So it’s good for accuracy, not for speaking.
A: And it needs data.
B: Then the library’s graded readers may suit you better.

blocks.x: The level check echoes the extensive reading principle of Unit 31. Resource evaluation extends the strategy training of Unit 19 into a durable skill.

body: Purpose: to give learners a memorable evaluation tool. Content: a magnifying glass over a book, a phone and a radio, with four labels around it: Level, Purpose, Quality, Habit. Style: clean icons with text labels. Board version: four words around a circle.

items: British Council LearnEnglish (free) and BBC Learning English (free) as sample resources to evaluate.
DIKSHA (free, Government of India) for curriculum-linked e-content.

blocks.x: The school or DIET library’s graded readers and newspapers, evaluated on a paper checklist.

pts: Teach specific self-monitoring techniques — error logs, reflective journals, can-do checklists — as concrete autonomous tools.
This connects directly to Unit 42's portfolio and reflective-writing principles, framed here as learner-driven rather than teacher-assigned.
Self-monitoring closes the loop between autonomous study and genuine, trackable improvement.

v: 20 minutes to set up; 5 minutes weekly

items: Learners divide a page into three columns: ‘What I wrote/said’, ‘Correct version’, ‘My rule or reminder’.
After each corrected piece of work, learners add two errors that were marked more than once.
Every fortnight, learners read their log, circle any error that appears three times, and choose one to work on.
Learners add a short journal entry: what they noticed and what they will do.
Keep a vocabulary log alongside the error log, with new words and example sentences.
Support: the teacher selects the two errors for each learner at first.
Challenge: learners classify their errors and look for patterns.

blocks.x: An error log (written for this book):

lines: He don’t like tea. → He doesn’t like tea. → he/she/it + doesn’t
discuss about the problem → discuss the problem → no ‘about’ after ‘discuss’
I noticed ‘discuss about’ three times this month. In Hindi we say ‘ke baare mein charcha karna’, so I add ‘about’. I will check every ‘discuss’ in my next essay.

blocks.x: The learner has moved from receiving correction to monitoring her own interlanguage (Unit 49). Unit 8 introduced the error log as a teacher tool; here it becomes learner-driven.

body: Purpose: to show a learner-owned monitoring tool. Content: an open notebook with a three-column error log and a small journal entry, a pencil circling one repeated error. Style: realistic, handwritten. Board version: a three-column table.

items: Google Docs (free) for a digital log that can be shared with the teacher.

blocks.x: The back pages of the English notebook.

body: Leni Dam’s learners kept logbooks in which they recorded what they had planned, what they had done and what they had learnt, and these became a focus for regular dialogue with the teacher (Dam 1995). The logbook worked because it was used every lesson, not occasionally.

pts: As autonomy develops, the teacher's role shifts from directing all learning decisions toward advising and supporting learner-made ones.
This shift should be gradual and explicit, not an abrupt withdrawal of support that leaves learners unprepared.
Learner-teacher conferences, discussing self-set goals and progress, support this transition well.

v: 5 minutes per learner, over two to three weeks

items: While the class works on a task, meet four or five learners each lesson at the teacher’s desk.
Each learner brings their goal page and error log.
Ask three questions: What is your goal? How is it going? What will you do next?
Offer advice only after the learner has spoken.
Note one agreed next step in the learner’s notebook and in your record.
In very large classes, hold group conferences with three learners who share a goal.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: T: What was your goal this month, Arjun?
S1: To speak more in group discussions.
T: How is it going?
S1: Better. But I only agree with people. I never give my own opinion.
T: What could you try?
S1: Prepare one opinion before the discussion?
T: Good. Let’s write that down as next week’s step.

blocks.x: Advising in language learning is now a recognized professional practice, with its own techniques of listening, questioning and restating (Mynard and Carson 2012). The shift from director to advisor should be gradual and explained to learners, so that they do not experience it as the teacher withdrawing support.

body: Purpose: to show the teacher’s changing role. Content: three frames: a teacher at the board; the teacher listening in a group; the teacher seated beside a learner who explains her own plan. Style: warm, story-like. Board version: three stick figures moving from front to side.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a conference record.

blocks.x: A conference notebook with one line per learner per meeting.

points.sub: Building it into the classroom itself
pts: Even within class time, offering genuine choices — of topic, of task approach, of resource — builds autonomous capacity incrementally.
This connects to Unit 36's project-based learning, where learner choice is already a core design principle.
Autonomy doesn't only develop outside class; classroom design itself can build or constrain it.

v: A choice board on the board or a handout

items: Draw a grid of six tasks, all practising the same language aim.
Vary the tasks by skill, format and difficulty.
Learners choose two tasks, including at least one from the lower row.
Learners complete them in pairs or individually.
Offer a choice of topic within a project (Unit 36).
Support: star the tasks with clearer models.
Challenge: learners design a seventh task for the board.

blocks.x: A choice board for describing a place (written for this book):

lines: Row 1: Write a postcard from Mysuru · Draw and label a map of your village · Describe a photo to a partner
Row 2: Write a tourist leaflet for your town · Record a one-minute guided tour · Compare two cities in a paragraph

blocks.x: In a class of fifty, the choice board is still manageable: the language aim is the same, the teacher monitors six task types rather than fifty plans, and learners experience real decisions. Autonomy-supportive teaching, which offers meaningful choice and explains the reasons for tasks, supports engagement (Reeve 2006).

body: Purpose: to show choice within structure. Content: a six-square grid of illustrated tasks under a banner naming the language aim, with learners’ hands reaching for different squares. Style: playful but ordered. Board version: a six-box grid.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for a digital choice board.

blocks.x: The grid drawn on the board or on chart paper.

pts: Expectations around learner independence versus teacher direction vary across educational cultures, connecting to Unit 24's intercultural awareness.
Build autonomy gradually and explicitly rather than assuming all learners arrive with the same expectations about their own role.
This isn't a reason to avoid teaching autonomy — it's a reason to teach it deliberately rather than assume it.

items: Give pairs a set of statements about who should do what in learning (see model language).
Pairs mark each statement: agree, disagree, not sure.
Discuss in groups: where do these expectations come from?
Explain gently why the course will ask learners to take on some teacher roles, and how you will support them.
Agree one new learner responsibility for the next month.
Discuss first in the home language for depth, then report in English.
Support: fewer statements with pictures.
Challenge: learners write a paragraph on how their view has changed.

lines: The teacher should correct every mistake.
Learners should choose some of their own reading.
Only the teacher knows whether my work is good.
S1: I think only the teacher knows if my work is good.
S2: But you can check spelling yourself. And you know if you understood a story.
T: Both points are true. I will still check your work. But I want you to be able to check some of it too.

blocks.x: Expectations about the teacher’s role vary across and within educational cultures (Palfreyman and Smith 2003), which connects with the intercultural awareness of Unit 24. Littlewood’s (1999) reactive autonomy is often the natural starting point: learners organize their own work towards goals the teacher sets, before setting goals themselves. Unit 56 develops advanced autonomy through learning contracts.

body: Purpose: to show autonomy developing from different cultural starting points. Content: paths from different villages and cities converging on a hilltop labelled ‘Taking charge of my learning’. Style: gentle landscape. Board version: several lines converging on a point.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) for an anonymous class vote on the statements.

blocks.x: Learners stand along an ‘agree–disagree’ line in the classroom or corridor.

body: Choose one class and share one decision with learners this week: let them choose between two reading texts, or set their own homework goal. Note who hesitates and who flourishes. Next month, share a second decision.

dek: Unit 48 of 100: moving beyond assessing autonomy readiness (Tier I) into actually building independent language-learning capability at the intermediate level.

aims.x: Unit 2 asked how ready learners were to work independently. Unit 47 suggested that independence is one of the best responses to the intermediate plateau. This unit turns readiness into practice: it treats learner autonomy as something a teacher teaches, step by step, through goal-setting, choosing resources, self-monitoring and a gradual change in the teacher’s own role.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: define learner autonomy and distinguish it from simply working alone;
explain why autonomy develops through practice and reflection rather than being a fixed trait;
teach goal-setting explicitly, building on micro-goals from Unit 47;
help learners evaluate self-study resources for level, purpose and quality;
introduce concrete self-monitoring tools such as error logs, learning journals and can-do checklists;
plan a gradual shift in your own role from director towards advisor;
build genuine choice into classroom tasks, even in large classes;
teach autonomy in ways that respect learners’ cultural expectations of teachers.

why: Why this matters. Autonomy is one of the most effective responses to the plateau this tier just addressed — and one of the most valuable long-term outcomes a course can produce.

background.x: The most widely cited definition of learner autonomy comes from Henri Holec, who described it as ‘the ability to take charge of one’s own learning’ (Holec 1981: 3 [VERIFY page]). Taking charge, for Holec, meant making the decisions a teacher usually makes: setting objectives, choosing content and methods, monitoring the process and evaluating the results. David Little (1991) added that autonomy is a capacity, including a psychological relationship to the process and content of learning, not a set of circumstances. Autonomy is about who decides, not where the learning happens.

Phil Benson (2011) reviews the research and concludes that autonomy is a capacity learners possess to differing degrees and that can be developed. Leni Dam’s (1995) long-running classroom work with Danish secondary learners showed how a teacher can build it through regular routines: learners keep logbooks, plan their own activities within a framework, and evaluate their work at set intervals, while the teacher moves gradually from directing to supporting.

Autonomy is sometimes described as a Western value that sits awkwardly in Asian classrooms. William Littlewood (1999) argued against this simple contrast, distinguishing proactive autonomy, where learners set their own direction, from reactive autonomy, where learners organize their own work towards a direction set by others; both are valuable, and learners in teacher-centred traditions often show the second readily. Indian policy is strongly supportive. NEP 2020 speaks of developing self-directed learners who can ‘learn how to learn’, and NCF 2023 emphasizes learner agency and choice (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). In multilingual classrooms learners already make sophisticated independent choices about which language to use for which purpose; autonomy in English learning can build on that expertise.

items: Decision audit. A completed ‘Who decides?’ grid for one class, before and after a month of changes.
Goal cycle. A learner’s four-week goal, weekly steps and review, showing adjustment.
Learner logs. Error logs and journal entries that show learners noticing and acting on patterns.
Conference record. Notes from a round of five-minute conferences, with agreed next steps.
In your classes, who makes most decisions about goals, content and evaluation?
Which of your learners already show reactive autonomy? Which show proactive autonomy?
How did you become an independent learner yourself? Who helped you?
What choices could you offer in a class of fifty without losing control of the lesson?
How do your learners’ families view the teacher’s role? How might that affect autonomy?
What would it feel like for you to become more of an advisor than a director?

terms.def: A professional practice in which an advisor helps learners reflect on and direct their own learning through dialogue, using techniques of listening, questioning and restating rather than instruction (Mynard and Carson 2012).

Teaching that nurtures learners’ sense of choice and ownership, for example by offering meaningful options, explaining reasons and acknowledging feelings, rather than controlling through pressure (Reeve 2006).
A record kept by the learner of their own errors, usually in three columns: what I wrote or said, the correct version, and my rule or reminder. It supports self-monitoring and learner autonomy.
Helping learners set specific, achievable learning goals, such as ‘use five new phrases in a conversation this week’, and review them. It is a core step in developing learner autonomy.

The capacity to take charge of one’s own learning, including setting goals, choosing materials and methods, and evaluating progress (Holec 1981); it is developed gradually, through guided choices, rather than simply handed over.

A regular written or recorded reflection in which learners note what they have learnt, what they found difficult and what they plan to do next; it supports reflection and autonomy, and may be written partly in the home language.

In Littlewood’s (1999) distinction, autonomy in which learners set their own direction, goals and methods, as opposed to reactive autonomy, where they organize their learning within a direction set by others.

Autonomy in which learners organize their own work towards goals the teacher has set, before they set goals themselves (Littlewood 1999). It is often the natural first step, for example learners choosing which graded reader to use for a teacher-set reading target.

The learner skill of judging self-study materials, such as apps, videos and books, for level, purpose and quality before using them. It is an important part of learner autonomy and extends earlier strategy training.

Learners keeping track of their own learning, such as progress towards goals, recurring errors or time spent, and adjusting their strategies accordingly. An error log is a common self-monitoring tool.
